abstract: Resolving displacements and surface irregularities far below a nanometer is now indispensable across fields, from precision manufacturing and biotechnology to nanoscience and fundamental metrology. High-precision optical interferometry reaches this $λ/1{,}000$ regime by reading out optical power, which provides a smooth response over the measurement range. Here we instead read out the complex dark-port field of a marginally imbalanced interferometer, whose phase response to small internal phase deviations $φ_{\textrm{in}}$ near destructive interference becomes extremely steep. For a small arm-amplitude imbalance $μ$, the tangent $T_{\textrm{out}}$ of the dark-port phase reduces to $μ^{-1}φ_{\textrm{in}}$, defining a phase magnification $M=μ^{-1}$. Crucially, this tangent estimator stays linear over a range $|φ_{\textrm{in}}|\lesssim\sqrt{|μ|}$---much larger than the imbalance $|μ|$ itself for $|μ|\ll1$---so that fine temporal substructure is resolved within much larger phase excursions. $T_{\textrm{out}}$ is synthesized from the dark-port complex field by optical time-domain holography and Fourier demodulation---a heterodyne readout that is intrinsically immune to laser relative-intensity noise at any magnification, and gives time-resolved access to phase dynamics. In a proof-of-principle Mach--Zehnder experiment, without optimization or environmental isolation, we demonstrate $|M|>10^3$ and optical-path resolution better than $λ/100{,}000$ ($\approx5~\textrm{pm}$), with a shot-noise floor orders of magnitude below this environment-limited value. The approach is compact, tunable, and compatible with existing interferometric platforms, offering a practical route to enhanced phase sensitivity in metrology, sensing, and optical instrumentation.
